title: Lay-led communities
hook: independent minyanim, where members lead prayer themselves

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: no label needed: some Jews choose no movement and simply describe what they do. On day seventeen you met the minyan, ten people praying together. Today, the rooms where those ten lead themselves.

A woman in a sweater gets up from a folding chair and begins the morning prayers. It's a rented room above a bookshop. A borrowed Torah scroll waits in a cabinet, beside a box of prayer books someone carried up the stairs. There's no rabbi on a stage, because there is no stage. Later a teenager reads from the Torah, nervous, carefully prepared. A retired dentist gives a five-minute thought on the week's portion. Next week, three different people will do those jobs. Groups like this go by a plain name: an independent minyan.
screen: `A WOMAN IN A SWEATER LEADS.` → `NO STAGE, NO PULPIT.` → `MEMBERS TAKE TURNS.`

segments.voice: Lay-led communities. Four turns. First, the quorum. A minyan is the group Jewish law asks for when a community prays together; the Mishnah lists prayers that are not said with fewer than ten. Streams differ on who counts toward the ten. What the law asks for is people, not a building and not a title. Second, the leader is a role, not a rank: the shaliach tzibbur, the messenger of the congregation. Jewish law does not require a rabbi for that job. Any member who knows the prayers can carry the room's words for a while, then sit back down. Third, the old picture behind it. At Sinai, the Torah says, God told the whole people: "ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation." Readers hear many things in that line. Some in lay-led groups hear a job description: the holiness belongs to everyone in the room, so the work can too. Fourth, the cost. Nobody is paid to do it, so somebody has to. Someone sets up the chairs, someone learns to chant a Torah portion, someone brings the food and stays to wash the cups. Independent minyanim vary a great deal: some egalitarian, some traditional, some in between. Some members also belong to a synagogue with a rabbi, and value both. What they share is the habit of handing the work around. A room like that exists because ordinary people decided to lead it.
screen: `THE LAW ASKS FOR PEOPLE.` · `A MESSENGER, NOT A RANK.` · `A KINGDOM OF PRIESTS.` · `SOMEONE SETS UP THE CHAIRS.` · then, large: `LAY-LED.`

segments.voice: Think of a group you already belong to: a household, a team, a few friends. Find one small job in it that usually waits for someone else, like starting the meal, picking the song, or opening a conversation that keeps getting postponed, and picture yourself doing it simply, without a speech. If you pray, offer the job up as you breathe; if not, just hold the picture steady.
Lay-led communities. Groups where members, not paid clergy, lead prayer, read Torah and teach, taking turns as the messenger of the congregation. Today's word.
Your line: lay-led. The room's words can be carried by anyone who knows them. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In independent minyanim, members take turns leading prayer, reading from the Torah and giving short teachings, and members share the practical work of setting up, hosting and cleaning up.
